front: State the RV basal diameter cutoff for RV dilation.
back: > 41 mm at the base in the RV-focused A4C view (mid > 35 mm). Measured with LV apex centered and the largest basal RV diameter shown.

front: State the RV wall thickness cutoff for RV hypertrophy.
back: > 5 mm at end-diastole (measured in the subcostal view or the RV free wall in the parasternal view).

front: List five ASE parameters for assessing RV systolic function and their cutoffs.
back: 1) RVEF < 45%. 2) RV FAC < 35%. 3) TAPSE < 17 mm. 4) RV S′ (TDI) < 9.5 cm/s. 5) RV GLS > −20% (less negative). 6) RIMP > 0.43 (PW) or > 0.54 (TDI).

front: Why is RVEF normally lower than LVEF even when SV is equal?
back: RV end-diastolic volume is larger than LV EDV (~87 mL/m² vs ~64 mL/m² in men). Since EF = SV / EDV, the same SV from a larger EDV produces a lower EF.

front: Why is TAPSE reduced after open-heart surgery even when RV function is preserved?
back: Pericardial adhesions restrict longitudinal (base-to-apex) motion. TAPSE reflects longitudinal displacement; radial function may be maintained.

front: Interventricular septal flattening in systole vs diastole — what does each indicate?
back: Systolic flattening: RV PRESSURE overload (PAH, PS). Diastolic flattening: RV VOLUME overload (ASD, severe TR/PR).
Akinesis of the RV free wall with SPARING of the apex (the apex still contracts vigorously due to LV tethering). Suggests acute pulmonary embolism / RV pressure overload.

front: Approximate PASP ceiling in acute massive PE?
back: ~60 mmHg. The thin-walled RV cannot acutely generate higher pressures; a value markedly above 60 suggests preexisting chronic PH.

front: State the RA area cutoff for RA enlargement.
back: > 18 cm² in the RV-focused A4C view (end-systole).

front: State the normal upper limits for TAPSE and RV S′.
back: TAPSE ≥ 17 mm. RV S′ (tissue Doppler tricuspid lateral annular systolic velocity) ≥ 9.5 cm/s.
RV FAC = (End-diastolic area − End-systolic area) / End-diastolic area × 100. Normal ≥ 35%.

front: Ebstein's anomaly — key echo criteria for the tricuspid valve.
back: Apical displacement of the septal leaflet by > 8 mm/m² (BSA-indexed) or > 20 mm in absolute terms, with atrialization of the proximal RV. Severe TR is common. Often associated with WPW.
Congenital absence (partial or complete) of RV myocardium, leaving a paper-thin RV. Rare. May mimic ARVC clinically.

front: What is the earliest echo finding of post-TOF repair to look for on follow-up?
back: Pulmonary regurgitation (from the RVOT patch) with progressive RV dilation. Long-term monitoring guides timing of pulmonary valve replacement (surgical or percutaneous).

front: Why is 3D RV imaging preferred over 2D when available?
back: The RV's complex crescent shape violates the geometric assumptions of 2D formulas. 3D provides direct volume measurement; correlates better with cMRI-derived RVEF.
